01_tensors_shapes.title: Tensors and Shapes
01_tensors_shapes.description: Most ML code manipulates tensors with shapes. Shape reasoning is the base layer for everything else.

q2.question: Why do shapes matter in ML code?
options: They only matter for plotting.
They determine which operations are valid and how data flows through layers.
They replace model parameters.
explanations: Shapes matter much more broadly than plotting.
Correct. Shape compatibility determines whether operations make sense.
Parameters are still needed.
q2.answerReason: A large share of ML debugging is really shape debugging.

q3.question: What is the main conceptual difference between a scalar and a vector?
options: A scalar is a single value; a vector is an ordered collection along one axis.
A scalar always lives on the CPU while a vector always lives on the GPU.
A vector cannot contain numbers.
explanations: Correct. Scalars and vectors differ by dimensional structure.
Device placement is separate.
Vectors are numeric collections.
q3.answerReason: Before architecture, you need a clear mental model of the data structures being transformed.

02_vector_dot.title: Dot Products
02_vector_dot.description: Many ML computations reduce to weighted sums, and the dot product is the simplest example.

q2.question: Why does the dot product appear constantly in ML models?
options: It forms the weighted-sum scoring core of linear layers and similarity calculations.
It is only used for image resizing.
It always produces probabilities.
explanations: Correct. Weighted sums and alignment scores show up everywhere.
It is much broader than image resizing.
Dot products are not probabilities by themselves.
q2.answerReason: Linear models and neural layers are built on this weighted-combination idea.

q3.question: Why is the dot product natural for a linear model?
options: Because it removes the need for weights.
Because it combines feature values and weights into one score.
Because it normalizes all features automatically.
explanations: Weights still matter.
Correct. Dot product is exactly a weighted sum across aligned dimensions.
Normalization is separate.
q3.answerReason: A linear model asks how much each feature should contribute to the score.

03_matrix_multiplication.title: Matrix Multiplication
03_matrix_multiplication.description: A dense neural layer is repeated dot products. Matrix multiplication is the batched version of linear scoring.

q2.question: Why is matrix multiplication central to neural networks?
options: It only formats tensors for printing.
It replaces loss functions.
It applies many weighted sums across inputs efficiently.
explanations: Formatting is unrelated.
Losses are still needed.
Correct. Linear layers are built from many weighted sums.
q2.answerReason: Dense layers become matrix operations because the same pattern repeats across neurons and batches.

q3.question: What does a shape mismatch usually mean here?
options: The intended dimensions for combining features and weights do not line up.
The optimizer is broken.
The GPU is always out of memory.
explanations: Correct. The dimensions do not agree for the operation you asked for.
Optimization is separate.
OOM is a different problem.
q3.answerReason: Many model bugs reduce to asking for an operation whose dimensions do not fit the intended mapping.

04_linear_regression_loss.title: Predictions Need Losses
04_linear_regression_loss.description: A model output becomes trainable only once you compare it with a target through a loss.

q2.question: Why is a loss function needed?
options: To convert tensors into strings.
To replace model parameters.
To measure how wrong the prediction is so learning has a direction.
explanations: Formatting is unrelated.
Parameters still exist.
Correct. Without a loss, there is no objective to improve.
q2.answerReason: Training needs a quantitative notion of error.

q3.question: What does squared error emphasize?
options: Larger mistakes become disproportionately more costly.
All mistakes cost exactly the same.
Only positive mistakes count.
explanations: Correct. Squaring magnifies larger residuals.
Squared error is not constant-cost.
Negative residuals also matter once squared.
q3.answerReason: The shape of the loss influences how strongly optimization reacts to different mistakes.

05_gradient_descent.title: Gradient Descent
05_gradient_descent.description: If the gradient points toward increasing loss, subtracting it moves parameters downhill locally.

q2.question: Why do we subtract the gradient during minimization?
options: Because gradients are always negative.
Because the gradient points toward increasing loss.
Because subtraction makes training deterministic.
explanations: Gradients can be positive, negative, or zero.
Correct. Moving opposite the gradient is the local downhill move.
Determinism depends on other factors too.
q2.answerReason: The sign matters because we want to reduce, not increase, the loss.

q3.question: What does the learning rate control?
options: Whether gradients exist at all.
Whether the loss is convex.
How large each parameter update step is.
explanations: Gradients come from the model and loss.
Convexity is a property of the landscape.
Correct. The learning rate scales the update.
q3.answerReason: Too small slows learning; too large can overshoot or destabilize it.

06_backprop_chain_rule.title: Backpropagation and the Chain Rule
06_backprop_chain_rule.description: Deep networks are compositions of functions, so gradients are propagated backward using the chain rule.

q2.question: Why is the chain rule central to backpropagation?
options: Because model outputs depend on nested intermediate computations.
Because it alphabetizes parameters.
Because it removes the need for a loss.
explanations: Correct. Composed functions require composed derivatives.
Alphabetical ordering is unrelated.
Loss is still required.
q2.answerReason: Neural nets are built from layers, so gradients must pass through one transformation after another.

q3.question: What is backprop fundamentally computing?
options: Only the final prediction.
How each parameter influenced the final loss through intermediate operations.
A new dataset.
explanations: Prediction happens in the forward pass.
Correct. Backprop traces influence backward through the graph.
It computes gradients, not data.
q3.answerReason: Updates work because parameters are judged by their contribution to error.

07_relu_sigmoid.title: Activations Add Nonlinearity
07_relu_sigmoid.description: Without nonlinear activations, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear transformation.

q2.question: Why are activation functions needed?
options: To sort training data.
To eliminate model parameters.
To let the network represent nonlinear relationships.
explanations: Sorting is unrelated.
Parameters still matter.
Correct. Nonlinearity is what makes deep networks expressive.
q2.answerReason: Without nonlinear activations, depth does not buy the behavior people want from neural networks.

q3.question: Why is ReLU often popular?
options: It is simple and avoids severe sigmoid-like saturation in many regions.
It converts every model into a probability distribution.
It guarantees perfect gradients everywhere.
explanations: Correct. ReLU is simple and often trains well.
Probabilities require other output choices.
ReLU still has zero-gradient regions.
q3.answerReason: Activation choice affects optimization behavior, not just output range.

08_softmax_cross_entropy.title: Softmax and Cross-Entropy
08_softmax_cross_entropy.description: Softmax turns logits into a normalized distribution, and cross-entropy scores how wrong that distribution is for the target class.

q2.question: Why do larger logits get larger softmax probabilities?
options: Softmax sorts classes alphabetically first.
Exponentiation preserves ordering and amplifies score differences before normalization.
Softmax clips all logits to the same value.
explanations: Class names do not control probability.
Correct. Bigger logits create bigger exponentials before normalization.
Softmax does not flatten every class equally.
q2.answerReason: Normalization rescales, but the exponential step makes high logits dominate more strongly.

q3.question: Why is softmax commonly paired with cross-entropy?
options: Because softmax alone trains the model automatically.
Because cross-entropy removes the need for logits.
Because one produces class probabilities and the other scores how wrong those probabilities are against the target.
explanations: Softmax does not provide the whole training objective.
Cross-entropy complements logits/probabilities.
Correct. Prediction distribution and training objective play complementary roles.
q3.answerReason: You need both a way to express confidence and a way to punish wrong confidence.

09_regularization.title: Regularization and Overfitting
09_regularization.description: Good training is not only about fitting the training set. Regularization helps control overfitting and improve generalization.

q2.question: Why is regularization used?
options: To reduce overfitting and improve generalization.
To remove the need for data.
To guarantee perfect accuracy.
explanations: Correct. Regularization constrains or perturbs learning to improve generalization.
Data is still essential.
No method guarantees perfection.
q2.answerReason: A model that memorizes training noise can look good on paper and fail in deployment.

q3.question: What does it usually mean if training loss is much lower than validation loss?
options: The optimizer is always broken.
The model may be overfitting the training data.
The dataset has no labels.
explanations: The optimizer may be fine.
Correct. This gap is a common overfitting signal.
Labels may exist just fine.
q3.answerReason: Generalization quality is measured on held-out data, not only on the training set.

10_optimizers.title: Optimizers
10_optimizers.description: Different optimizers update parameters differently, even though they all use gradient information.

q2.question: Why do optimizers differ if they all use gradients?
options: Because gradients are optional.
Because only Adam uses learning rates.
Because they store and transform gradient history differently when deciding updates.
explanations: Gradients are the core input.
Many optimizers use learning rates.
Correct. Update rules differ in how they use current and past gradient information.
q2.answerReason: An optimizer is an update policy, not just a gradient transport mechanism.

q3.question: Why does optimizer choice matter?
options: It affects stability, convergence speed, and how training behaves across different objectives.
It changes tokenization rules.
It removes the need for batching.
explanations: Correct. Update policy shapes training dynamics.
Tokenization is unrelated.
Batching is still useful.
q3.answerReason: Optimization is not only about correctness; it is also about training behavior.

11_batching_normalization.title: Batching and Normalization
11_batching_normalization.description: Mini-batches improve throughput, and normalization techniques can stabilize activations or gradient flow in deep models.

q2.question: Why use mini-batches?
options: They improve hardware utilization and provide more efficient gradient estimates per step.
They make losses unnecessary.
They guarantee perfect generalization.
explanations: Correct. Batching is a systems and statistics choice.
Losses are still essential.
Generalization is not guaranteed by batching.
q2.answerReason: Batching affects both hardware efficiency and optimization noise.

q3.question: Why are normalization layers often useful?
options: They replace all model parameters.
They remove the need for activations.
They can make training dynamics more stable by controlling representation scale or distribution.
explanations: Normalization complements parameters; it does not replace them.
Activations still matter.
Correct. Stabilizing internal representations can improve optimization.
q3.answerReason: Training deep models is partly an optimization problem, not only an architecture problem.

12_tokenization.title: Tokenization
12_tokenization.description: Language models do not ingest raw strings directly. Text is broken into tokens and tokens map to integer ids.

q2.question: Why does tokenization matter before training an LLM?
options: The model needs discrete units it can embed, score, and predict.
It is only for pretty-printing outputs.
It removes the need for a vocabulary.
explanations: Correct. Tokenization defines the discrete symbols the model operates over.
It is part of the model pipeline, not just output formatting.
Tokenization and vocabulary are tightly connected.
q2.answerReason: Before embeddings or attention, the model needs a workable discrete representation of text.

q3.question: What tradeoff does tokenization influence?
options: Only GPU fan speed.
Vocabulary size, sequence length, and what patterns are represented compactly.
Whether gradients exist.
explanations: Hardware fan speed is irrelevant.
Correct. Token granularity has real modeling and efficiency consequences.
Gradients are a training property, not a tokenizer property.
q3.answerReason: Different tokenizers change how much structure each symbol carries and how long sequences become.

13_embeddings.title: Embeddings
13_embeddings.description: A token id is just an index. An embedding layer maps that index into a learned dense vector.

q2.question: Why is an embedding layer needed?
options: Because token ids are already meaningful geometric vectors.
Because it converts gradients into text.
Because the model needs learned continuous representations rather than arbitrary numeric ids.
explanations: Token ids are arbitrary identifiers, not geometry.
Embeddings are about representation, not text conversion.
Correct. Learned vectors create a useful space for similarity and composition.
q2.answerReason: Embedding lookup is the bridge from discrete symbols to continuous computation.

q3.question: Why would raw token ids be a bad representation?
options: The numeric closeness of ids is arbitrary and does not represent semantic similarity.
Ids are always too large to fit in memory.
Raw ids automatically create attention weights.
explanations: Correct. Id numbers are labels, not learned meaning.
Memory is not the core conceptual issue.
Attention needs vector representations to compare meaningfully.
q3.answerReason: Embeddings let the model learn structure instead of inheriting meaningless integer distances.

14_positional_encoding.title: Position Must Be Represented
14_positional_encoding.description: Self-attention alone does not inherently know token order. Position information must be injected so the model can distinguish sequence order.

q2.question: Why is positional information needed in transformers?
options: Because token ids are too short.
Because attention compares items in a set-like way unless order information is added.
Because it removes the need for embeddings.
explanations: Token id length is not the key issue.
Correct. Without positional signal, order is not directly encoded.
Embeddings are still needed.
q2.answerReason: Transformers need an explicit way to represent sequence order.

q3.question: What problem appears if a model has no useful positional signal?
options: It can struggle to distinguish sequences that contain the same tokens in different orders.
It forgets how to multiply matrices.
It stops producing logits.
explanations: Correct. Order-sensitive meaning becomes hard to represent.
Matrix multiplication is unrelated.
The architecture can still produce logits.
q3.answerReason: Language meaning often depends on order, so order must appear in the representation.

15_attention_scores.title: Attention Scores
15_attention_scores.description: Self-attention begins by comparing a query vector with key vectors. Larger scores usually mean greater relevance.

q2.question: What does a larger query-key score usually mean?
options: The query is more aligned with that key, so that token can receive more attention weight.
The sequence becomes shorter.
The model skips the value vectors.
explanations: Correct. Scores rank relevance before normalization.
Scores do not change sequence length directly.
Values are still needed for the final weighted mix.
q2.answerReason: The score is not the output itself; it is the relevance signal used to compute weights.

q3.question: Why are raw attention scores usually followed by softmax?
options: To remove the need for value vectors.
To change keys into labels.
To turn relative relevance scores into normalized attention weights.
explanations: Values are still needed after scoring.
Scores are not labels.
Correct. Softmax converts scores into a usable weighting distribution.
q3.answerReason: Raw comparisons become useful mixing coefficients only after normalization.

16_scaled_masked_attention.title: Scaling and Masking
16_scaled_masked_attention.description: Transformers usually scale attention scores and may apply masks before softmax.

q2.question: Why divide attention scores by `sqrt(d_k)`?
options: To convert the model into a CNN.
To keep score magnitudes from growing too large as vector dimension increases.
To remove the need for softmax.
explanations: Architecture type is unrelated.
Correct. Large dot products can make softmax too peaky.
Softmax is still used.
q2.answerReason: Score scaling is a numerical-stability trick tied to vector dimensionality.

q3.question: What is the purpose of a causal mask in autoregressive decoding?
options: It prevents a position from attending to future tokens that should not yet be visible.
It forces every token to attend equally to all previous tokens.
It removes tokenization from the model.
explanations: Correct. Autoregressive training and generation require hiding future information.
Masks constrain visibility; they do not equalize weights.
Tokenization is separate.
q3.answerReason: Without a causal mask, next-token prediction would leak future information backward into earlier positions.

17_multi_head_attention.title: Multi-Head Attention
17_multi_head_attention.description: Multiple heads let the model project into multiple subspaces and capture different relationships in parallel.

q2.question: Why use multiple attention heads instead of one?
options: To eliminate embeddings.
To make every head compute the same pattern redundantly.
To let the model capture different relationships in parallel subspaces.
explanations: Embeddings are still required.
The point is diversity, not redundancy.
Correct. Different heads can specialize in different signals.
q2.answerReason: Multi-head attention increases representational flexibility.

q3.question: What usually happens after per-head attention outputs are computed?
options: They are deleted immediately.
They are combined, often by concatenation followed by a learned projection.
They are turned into tokenizer rules.
explanations: The outputs are used, not discarded.
Correct. Multi-head structure eventually merges back into one stream.
Tokenization is separate.
q3.answerReason: Heads are useful because their outputs are recombined into a richer representation.

18_transformer_block.title: Transformer Block Structure
18_transformer_block.description: A transformer block typically includes attention, residual connections, normalization, and a feed-forward network.

q2.question: Why are residual connections important?
options: They let layers learn corrections on top of existing representations instead of rebuilding everything from scratch.
They remove the need for nonlinear operations.
They force every layer to compute the exact same function.
explanations: Correct. Residual learning improves optimization and information flow.
Residuals complement, not replace, nonlinear layers.
Layers can still learn different transformations.
q2.answerReason: Residual paths help deep networks preserve signal while adding refinements gradually.

q3.question: Why is the feed-forward network still important after attention?
options: Because attention cannot produce vectors.
Because it tokenizes the input again.
Because attention mixes information across positions, while the feed-forward sublayer applies learned nonlinear transformation at each position.
explanations: Attention does produce vectors.
The transformer does not re-tokenize here.
Correct. The block needs both cross-position mixing and per-position transformation capacity.
q3.answerReason: Attention is not the whole transformer; the feed-forward part adds substantial modeling power.

19_pretraining_objective.title: Pretraining Objective
19_pretraining_objective.description: Pretraining gives the model broad language competence by optimizing a large-scale prediction objective across diverse text.

q2.question: Why is large-scale pretraining powerful?
options: Because every token becomes supervised signal conditioned on context.
Because it memorizes one fixed answer for each prompt length.
Because it removes the need for an objective.
explanations: Correct. The text itself provides dense supervision token by token.
Generalization is broader than memorizing one answer per length.
The prediction objective is exactly what drives learning.
q2.answerReason: Pretraining works because natural text provides massive conditional prediction signal.

q3.question: What does pretraining primarily give the model before task-specific tuning?
options: A guarantee of perfect factuality.
A broad internal representation of language patterns and world-correlated textual structure.
A fixed one-line answer for every question.
explanations: Pretraining does not guarantee perfect truthfulness.
Correct. It builds broad statistical competence rather than certainty.
Generation stays dynamic and context-dependent.
q3.answerReason: Pretraining is about broad representation learning, not hard-coded lookup.

20_fine_tuning.title: Fine-Tuning
20_fine_tuning.description: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model toward a narrower task, dataset, style, or behavior objective.

q2.question: Why fine-tune a pretrained model instead of always training from scratch?
options: Because pretraining is useless.
Because fine-tuning removes the need for data.
Because it reuses broad pretrained structure and adapts it to a narrower objective more efficiently.
explanations: Pretraining is highly valuable.
Fine-tuning still depends on suitable data and objectives.
Correct. Reuse of broad prior structure is the major advantage.
q2.answerReason: Fine-tuning stands on top of pretrained competence instead of rebuilding everything from zero.

q3.question: What is the main role of fine-tuning in a model pipeline?
options: To steer a broadly capable model toward more specific behavior or tasks.
To remove all need for evaluation.
To delete the pretrained representation.
explanations: Correct. Fine-tuning is adaptation, not total replacement.
Evaluation is still necessary.
The pretrained structure is usually the starting point.
q3.answerReason: Fine-tuning narrows and reshapes broad capability rather than creating it from nothing.

21_evaluation_metrics.title: Evaluation Metrics
21_evaluation_metrics.description: You cannot judge a model only by training loss. Real systems need task-appropriate metrics and evaluation sets.

q2.question: Why are explicit evaluation metrics needed?
options: Because models cannot produce numbers.
Because the notion of “good” depends on the task.
Because evaluation removes the need for datasets.
explanations: Models do produce numeric outputs.
Correct. Good performance must be defined against task-appropriate criteria.
Evaluation still requires data.
q2.answerReason: A model can optimize one number and still fail the thing you care about.

q3.question: Why can training loss alone be misleading?
options: A lower training loss does not necessarily imply good behavior on held-out data or the real task objective.
Training loss directly measures human preference.
Training loss and deployment quality are always identical.
explanations: Correct. Generalization and task success must be checked separately.
Human preference is a different evaluation dimension.
They are not automatically identical.
q3.answerReason: You need evaluation that measures the behavior you truly want, not just the optimization target.

22_inference_sampling.title: Inference and Sampling
22_inference_sampling.description: At inference time, logits must be decoded into token choices. Decoding strategy changes style, diversity, and determinism.

q2.question: Why does decoding strategy matter?
options: Because choosing among token probabilities affects diversity, determinism, and output behavior.
Because it changes the training dataset retroactively.
Because it removes the need for logits.
explanations: Correct. Sampling, greedy decoding, and related strategies shape generation behavior.
Inference does not rewrite training data.
Logits are still the starting point.
q2.answerReason: Model output is not only about the learned parameters; it is also about how token choices are made at inference time.

q3.question: What is a common tradeoff when increasing generation randomness?
options: It guarantees more factual answers.
It may increase diversity while also increasing the chance of wandering or unstable outputs.
It disables the vocabulary.
explanations: Randomness does not guarantee factuality.
Correct. Diversity and stability often trade off.
The vocabulary still exists.
q3.answerReason: Decoding is part of product behavior, not just a technical afterthought.

23_rlhf_alignment.title: Alignment and Preference Optimization
23_rlhf_alignment.description: Modern assistant-like behavior is shaped not only by pretraining, but also by later objectives based on human preference or instruction-following targets.

q2.question: Why add preference-based post-training after pretraining?
options: Because pretraining already optimizes exactly for assistant helpfulness and safety.
Because alignment removes the need for evaluation.
Because raw next-token prediction alone does not fully specify the behavior users want from an assistant.
explanations: Pretraining gives broad capability, not the full target behavior profile.
Evaluation is still necessary.
Correct. Post-training helps steer capability toward desired behavior.
q2.answerReason: Capability and desirable behavior are related but not identical objectives.

q3.question: What is the core idea behind preference-based training?
options: Use signals about which outputs are preferred to push the model toward more desirable behavior.
Delete the pretrained model entirely.
Make logits disappear.
explanations: Correct. Preferences become an additional training signal.
The pretrained model is adapted, not discarded.
Logits remain part of the model’s internal scoring.
q3.answerReason: Alignment methods add another layer of objective shaping beyond plain next-token prediction.

24_data_quality.title: Data Quality and Curation
24_data_quality.description: Model quality depends strongly on data quality. Bad labels, noisy samples, leakage, or skewed distributions can corrupt learned behavior.

q2.question: Why is data quality central to model quality?
options: Because data never affects what the model learns.
Because the model can only learn patterns present, emphasized, or mislabeled in the data.
Because better data eliminates the need for architecture.
explanations: Data is exactly what the model learns from.
Correct. Data quality shapes learned behavior deeply.
Architecture still matters.
q2.answerReason: A strong model trained on weak or corrupted data can still learn weak or corrupted behavior.

q3.question: What is data leakage in evaluation?
options: A GPU overheating event.
A tokenizer with too many subwords.
Information from evaluation or future data sneaking into training or feature construction, making results look better than they really are.
explanations: Hardware heat is unrelated.
Tokenizer size is unrelated.
Correct. Leakage creates falsely optimistic evaluation.
q3.answerReason: Leakage is dangerous because it can make a model look far better than it will behave in real deployment.

25_rag_systems.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
25_rag_systems.description: Some LLM systems retrieve external documents at inference time so generation can condition on fresher or narrower context than pretraining alone provides.

q2.question: Why use retrieval in an LLM system?
options: To inject relevant external context at inference time instead of relying only on model parameters.
To remove the need for tokenization.
To make the model stop using attention.
explanations: Correct. Retrieval can add fresh or domain-specific context.
Tokenization is still required.
Attention still matters.
q2.answerReason: Retrieval is a systems design choice that complements parametric model knowledge.

q3.question: What problem is RAG often trying to improve?
options: How many colors the UI uses.
Grounding answers in specific retrieved context rather than relying only on the model’s internal memory.
Whether matrix multiplication exists.
explanations: UI color is unrelated.
Correct. Retrieval can improve specificity and grounding when the right documents are found.
Linear algebra is unrelated.
q3.answerReason: RAG is partly a knowledge access architecture, not only a model-weights story.

26_inference_efficiency.title: Inference Efficiency
26_inference_efficiency.description: Serving large models is a systems problem involving memory footprint, throughput, latency, batching, caching, and hardware utilization.

q2.question: Why is inference efficiency a separate engineering concern from model quality?
options: Because better models never cost more to serve.
Because serving only depends on UI design.
Because even a strong model can be impractical if latency, memory, or throughput are unacceptable.
explanations: Better models may cost substantially more to serve.
Serving is far more than UI work.
Correct. Deployment quality includes systems constraints.
q2.answerReason: A model’s usefulness depends on whether it can run within real product constraints.

q3.question: What is batching during inference often trying to improve?
options: Hardware utilization and throughput by serving multiple requests together when appropriate.
How the tokenizer splits words.
Whether gradients exist.
explanations: Correct. Batching can improve throughput, though latency tradeoffs may appear.
Tokenization is separate.
Gradients are not the issue at inference.
q3.answerReason: Serving design is about tradeoffs between throughput, latency, and resource usage.

27_failure_modes.title: Failure Modes and Limits
27_failure_modes.description: Good curricula must cover what models do wrong too: hallucination, overconfidence, distribution shift, reward hacking, and brittle generalization.

q2.question: Why study failure modes explicitly?
options: Because failures are irrelevant once the model trains.
Because understanding limits is necessary for evaluation, deployment safety, and realistic expectations.
Because failure modes only exist in small models.
explanations: Failures matter throughout deployment.
Correct. Model capability without limit-awareness is not enough.
Large models have failure modes too.
q2.answerReason: A real curriculum should teach where the model breaks, not only where it works.

q3.question: What is hallucination in LLM behavior?
options: Confidently producing unsupported or fabricated content that sounds plausible.
A faster matrix multiply.
A type of optimizer step.
explanations: Correct. Hallucination is a behavior problem in generated content.
Linear algebra speed is unrelated.
Optimization is unrelated.
q3.answerReason: A model can sound coherent and still be wrong, which is why evaluation and grounding matter.

28_end_to_end_view.title: End-to-End View
28_end_to_end_view.description: A modern AI system is not only a model. It is data, preprocessing, objective, optimization, evaluation, inference, and product constraints working together.

q2.question: Why is an end-to-end perspective important?
options: Because model behavior comes from the whole pipeline, not only from one architecture diagram.
Because architecture never matters.
Because data can be ignored once training starts.
explanations: Correct. Real systems emerge from many linked choices.
Architecture still matters a lot.
Data remains foundational.
q2.answerReason: A model is one component inside a larger training and deployment system.

q3.question: What is the main lesson of a full AI curriculum compared with an intro-only one?
options: That all models are basically the same.
That understanding real systems requires connecting math, data, architecture, optimization, and deployment behavior.
That only tokenization matters.
explanations: A serious curriculum should distinguish many important components.
Correct. Broad understanding comes from connecting the pieces.
Tokenization is only one part.
q3.answerReason: The whole curriculum is about the connections between components, not isolated vocabulary words.

30_overfitting_generalization.title: Overfitting and Generalization
30_overfitting_generalization.description:
A model can fit the training set well yet generalize poorly to unseen data.

```text
train good != deploy good
```

Generalization is a core ML goal, not a side detail.

q2.question: What is overfitting?
options: Having too few parameters.
Using a GPU for training.
Learning the training set too specifically and failing to generalize well.
explanations: Too few parameters is a different issue.
Hardware choice is unrelated.
Correct. Overfitting is a generalization failure.
q2.answerReason: A model can look strong on training data and still fail on new examples.

q3.question: Why is this a deployment concern?
options: Because production only uses the training set.
Because real users send unseen inputs, not the exact training distribution slice you optimized on.
Because overfitting changes Python syntax.
explanations: Production inputs are not just the training set.
Correct. Deployment quality depends on unseen data behavior.
Syntax is unrelated.
q3.answerReason: Real systems care about how the model behaves beyond the training set.

34_hallucination_grounding.title: Hallucination and Grounding
34_hallucination_grounding.description:
A language model can produce fluent output that is still wrong.

```text
confidence != correctness
```

Reliable systems need grounding, evaluation, and product constraints around the model.

q2.question: Why is hallucination mitigation not only a prompt-writing problem?
options: Because retrieval quality, evaluation, tool use, and product constraints also shape factual behavior.
Because hallucinations disappear at temperature zero.
Because only users cause hallucinations.
explanations: Correct. System design matters too.
That is too strong.
Users are not the only factor.
q2.answerReason: Prompts matter, but reliable factual behavior usually needs broader system design.

q3.question: What does grounding try to improve?
options: How many fonts the UI uses.
Only GPU memory usage.
Whether outputs stay tied to evidence or trusted context rather than unsupported guesses.
explanations: Fonts are unrelated.
GPU memory is a different concern.
Correct. Grounding is about evidence-backed behavior.
q3.answerReason: Grounding reduces unsupported generation by tying answers to better context.
